newsitem.title: INDIA: India to ease foreign investment rules for mining.
newsitem.headline: India to ease foreign investment rules for mining.

text.p: India plans to simplify and streamline regulatory procedures in the mining sector to attract foreign private investment, senior government officials told an international seminar on Saturday.

Federal Steel and Mines Minister B.P. Baishya said a committee of senior officials was examining how to streamline the grant of prospecting licences and mining leases as well as to suggest measures to reduce delays in approving them.

"I am sure these policy changes would go a long way in promoting the exploration and development of mineral resources in the country, as well give a further boost to mineral-based industries," Baishya said.
Mines Secretary B.B. Tandon said the committee, which is expected to submit its report soon, will suggest necessary amendments to mining laws.

"It is possible to attract large private investment and foreign capital along with state-of-the-art technology in exploration and mining with the active participation of state governments," Tandon said.
He said the common mimimum programme of India's United Front government had envisaged a annual direct foreign investment of $100 billion.
"Exploration and mining is an area which can attract sizeable foreign investment," Tandon said.
In recent months, nearly three dozen foreign investment proposals in mining, totalling $500 million had been approved by the government, he said.
"There are excellent geological prospects to find new deposits as the country has not fully explored its resources using modern techniques," Tandon said.
These opportunities included evaluation and development of a number of small primary gold deposits based on preliminary investigations, he said.

"The potential for discovering new gold deposits is high," Tandon added. "Numerous places in southern India have indicated the presence of several primary sources that are yet to be fully identified."
Tandon said other areas for investment would be joint ventures in copper, lead and zinc mining.

India opened up its mining sector to private and foreign investment in March 1993 as part of a programme of economic reforms that began to tear down the protectionist walls of a decades-old socialist economy in 1991.
As many as 13 minerals, which were earlier reserved for state-owned units were "dereserved" and restrictions on foreign investment were removed.
To boost confidence among foreign investors, the government also set up mining tribunals to resolve disputes.

In October 1996, the government issued guidelines to facilitate automatic approval of ventures involving foreign equity participation up to 50 percent. It also raised the ceiling govering the area for prospecting to 5,000 sq km from 25 sq km.
The chief minister of the western state of Maharashtra, Monohar Joshi, who also addressed the seminar, said the progress of private investment in mining had been extremely slow in the recent past.
"Foreign investors also took a pause," Joshi said. "The problems are mainly procedural. Summary procedures to speed up investment need to be evolved."
